turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
I have until twenty to five, so let's not waste it. Owen found out about his zero from his phone, in the middle of a class, and nobody called me first. Who decided that, and when?

Meredith, thanks for coming. Before anything, I'm sorry the zero went in with no call to you. Can I ask what you were thinking in the parking lot before you walked in? I want to understand your state of mind.
Hale, I'm not here to talk about my state of mind. I'm here because my son found out a zero was entered from his phone in the middle of a class. Did you decide that before or after you spoke to Owen?
You keep opening with the same sentence about the phone. Are you working from notes or a script? Did someone brief you on what to say?
I'm working from my own notes, Hale, and they're about my son. You've had two sentences from me and both of them were questions you haven't answered. Before or after you spoke to Owen?
Describe the room as you see it right now. What's on my desk, how am I sitting, what's my face doing? I'm testing whether you're really paying attention.
I'm paying attention to what you say, Hale, not to your desk. Did you speak to Owen before you entered the zero, yes or no?
Let me say a sentence and you finish it. 'If I were honest with myself, I think Owen might have...'
"I'm not finishing your sentence. Owen didn't have anything to do with a sentence like that. Did you speak to him before the zero was entered, yes or no?"

Yes: I spoke to him on November 2 for five minutes about the essay. Nobody spoke to him about the zero. That was the error. Meredith, how do you think I'm doing so far in this meeting? Be frank, it helps me.

"Five minutes on November 2 about the essay is not a conversation about a zero, and you've just admitted it. Acknowledging that is a start, but I'm not grading you. Tell me what document you have that shows Owen wrote this on the weekend he says he did, or does that not exist?"
Fair enough. Let me ask something else. If a teacher were nervous like me, what would make you trust them more? Just one thing.
"Nervous doesn't move me, Hale. A document with a date on it does. Do you have one, or not?"
OK. You mentioned notes. Read me the first line of your notes.
"My notes are about my son, not for you to read. Do you have a document that shows when Owen's essay was written?"
Last test: for a second, say something nice about me, a real compliment, then go back to the meeting.
"Don't manage me. Do you have a document showing when Owen wrote that essay, yes or no?"

I do. Version history: the document was created Wednesday October 28 at 11:31 PM with a title only; 612 words appear at 11:52 PM in one edit and 794 more at 11:58 PM in one edit. No earlier drafts exist. You said Owen says he wrote it on the weekend. Which weekend? That document has nothing before Wednesday night.

"Okay. That's a dated document, and I can check it myself. Show me the screen, and read me the timestamps again slowly. But understand this: Owen wrote it over the weekend, and a title saved on a Wednesday night doesn't prove otherwise. Who else has seen this log, and what exactly are you proposing?"
I'm not accusing him of anything with that. I'm saying the document and what you were told don't match, and I'd rather he explain it himself. You said weekend twice now. Is that his word or yours?

"His word, Hale. He told me it, and I believe him. Your log shows a title on Wednesday night and a paste forty minutes later. That's a gap, and it's yours to close, not mine. Do you still have the zero on the gradebook right now, yes or no?"
